hypotheses.name: IRGC captured the succession (weak form — assessed finding)
hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Trump threatens Iran's deepest nuclear site as satellites show work
brief.h: Trump said American intelligence is watching Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La - the tunnel complex two kilometres south of Natanz that Western analysts call Pickaxe Mountain - and advised Iran 'not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard', while also saying the conflict would not end until after November's midterm elections; the warning follows a CSIS study of 9 July Airbus and 9 August Satellogic imagery finding more road activity at the site in 2026 than at any point in its history and the south and east tunnel portals visibly more hardened than in September 2025, and it landed on a day Iran struck ships near the Strait of Hormuz after US missiles hit five Iranian tankers, with transits falling to seven against a ten-day average of fourteen.
brief.t: The load-bearing fact about Pickaxe Mountain is that nobody has a weapon for it. The main chambers sit at least a hundred metres under granite, the portals are cut in a U-bend specifically so a penetrator cannot fly straight down the corridor, and the GBU-57 was sized against Fordow's depth rather than this one. So read the threat as an instrument rather than a targeting decision: naming a site you cannot destroy is how you price a negotiation without spending a bomb. Then notice what the announcement actually moved - Brent went through $105 the same afternoon and Hormuz transits halved - which means this threat is being underwritten by shipowners and refiners, not by the Iranian nuclear programme. And notice the sentence that got less attention than the threat: the war ends after the midterms is a schedule, not an assessment.
brief.context: The rail predates the headline by six years. Excavation at Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La began in 2020 as an explicit hedge against exactly this - a hardened safe haven for the programme, built while the JCPOA's collapse was still being litigated - and Iran completed the security perimeter fence around the entire facility between June and September 2025, after the first American strikes. The desk that decides is not the podium; it is whoever owns the deep-penetration munition inventory and the Hormuz escalation ladder, because a strike on Pickaxe has to be paid for in tanker traffic. The base rate on this specific threat is the most useful number on the card: this site has now been publicly threatened in July, on 5 September and again today, and it has not been struck - announced-and-not-executed is running three for three. What would change the read is the one thing the analysts refused to claim. CSIS states plainly that its assessment 'can neither refute nor substantiate' the Israeli intelligence claim that centrifuges were moved in, and notes that the continuous construction combined with the ABSENCE of a heightened internal security posture suggests the site is not yet capable of enrichment work. Confirmation that enrichment has started there converts a bargaining threat into a target.

angles.effect: gains - a coercive lever that costs nothing to hold, reprices oil and Tehran's negotiating position on announcement alone, and can be repeated indefinitely
gains, partly - every un-executed threat cheapens the next one and validates the line foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei used in July, that the file is 'a fabricated pretext for aggression'

angles.party: The IAEA and the inspection regime
angles.effect: pays - the agency has had no visibility since June 2025 and says it cannot report the size, location or composition of Iran's roughly 440kg of 60 per cent material; threats keep inspectors out
pay - the threat transmits through war-risk premia and Hormuz transit counts, which is a bill sent to freight rather than to Natanz
pay - a strike they cannot veto creates a retaliation address they cannot move

dec.kill: Confirmation from the IAEA, or imagery showing the heightened internal security posture CSIS says is currently missing, that enrichment or centrifuge operation has begun inside Pickaxe. That converts announcement into targeting and this read is wrong. Conversely a fourth public threat that passes without a strike should be scored as an instrument, not an intention.

consp.claim: That the Pickaxe threat is theatre with a calendar attached. The mountain cannot be cracked - posters put it as 'there is no weapon on earth that can crack over 100 metres of granite' - so the point of naming it is the naming, and the tell is Trump saying the war will not end until after the election, which drew the direct question 'how does he know?'. A parallel strand treats an Israeli Channel 13 report that the IDF has now 'seen movement at Pickaxe Mountain' as a trigger being placed in advance of a strike decision already taken, and a third simply reads the whole sequence as oil-price management timed to the midterm calendar.
consp.spread: /pol/'s Persia-Israel general, now on edition 2,095 and past 300 replies, carried all three readings through the afternoon alongside a running day-counter mocking the war's duration - day 195 of what the thread calls the four-day special military operation.
consp.read: This maps onto the wag-the-dog frame, and it has two checkable kernels and one weak joint. The kernels are real: Trump did publicly put the end of the conflict after November, which is a schedule offered as a forecast, and the physics objection is close to correct - CSIS puts the main chambers at least 100 metres down behind U-bend portals built to defeat penetrators. The weak joint is the inference from un-strikeable to therefore-staged. The boring explanation covers it: a threat you cannot execute is still a cheap way to price a negotiation, which is exactly what the oil tape did within the hour.

brief.head: Houthis push on the Hanish islands as Iran promises more weapons
brief.h: After taking Mocha and the Hais district on Thursday, Ansar Allah pressed Dhubab and began attacking the Hanish islands, holding coastline within fifty miles of a strait about twenty kilometres wide that carries roughly a tenth of world seaborne trade; France 24 reported that Revolutionary Guards gave direct guidance to the coastal advance and that Tehran has promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to escalate strikes on Saudi Arabia, while Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam continued to insist navigation at Bab el-Mandeb remains safe and regular. Vessel transits at the Strait of Hormuz fell to seven on Wednesday against a ten-day average of fourteen.
brief.t: The reason to rewrite this card six hours after writing it is that the story changed owner. A Houthi land advance is a Yemeni civil war event; a Houthi land advance guided by Revolutionary Guards officers and resupplied on a promise of Iranian weapons is a second front, and second fronts are bought for what they do to the price of the FIRST one. Tehran is under bombardment at Kharg and Jask, is watching its tanker fleet struck, and has just been told publicly that its deepest facility is on a target list. Opening a second chokepoint costs it no Iranian materiel and no Iranian casualties, and it raises the price of every American demand at Hormuz. That is why Abdulsalam keeps saying the strait is safe - a chokepoint you close pays once, a chokepoint you can close pays continuously.
brief.context: The rail is the 2022 UN truce, which froze a front line rather than ending a war, and the specific weakness it froze in place: the western coast has been held since 2018 not by the internationally recognised government but by Tareq Saleh's National Resistance, an Emirati-built force nominally on the government's side and never integrated into it - which is why a withdrawal there produces a reorganisation rather than a counterattack. The desk that decides whether this becomes a world event is the London marine war-risk market, not Riyadh's foreign ministry, because the conversion happens when protection-and-indemnity cover reprices, and that is triggered by underwriter perception rather than by an attack. The base rate is the discipline here: through 2024 and 2025 the Houthis fired on shipping for more than a year without ever closing Bab el-Mandeb. What would change the read is a strike on a hull with no Saudi connection - Lloyd's List Intelligence reports the industry's working assumption is still that the threat is confined to Saudi-linked tonnage, and that belief is the only thing holding transits near 273 a week against a pre-blockade 319.

angles.effect: gains - a Red Sea card that raises the price of any Hormuz settlement, paid for in Yemeni manpower rather than Iranian
gains - coastline that turns coercion into a standing asset requiring no missile, plus the standing it needs inside Yemen
pays - the client force it underwrote on the western coast has lost the coast, closing the exit ramp from a war Riyadh has been trying to leave since 2022

angles.party: Yemeni civilians on the Red Sea coast
angles.effect: pay - a front line moving through populated ports with aid access already degraded
pay - the Cape reroute adds roughly ten days to a voyage whether or not a shot is fired, and Bab el-Mandeb war-risk already sits at 0.5 per cent of hull value

dec.kill: An attack on a hull with no Saudi link, or a Bab el-Mandeb war-risk quotation that stops distinguishing Saudi-linked tonnage from the general trade. Either ends the reading that this is leverage rather than blockade. Conversely, weekly transits holding near 270 through end-September confirms the advance bought position, not closure.

consp.claim: That the speed is impossible without a hidden hand. Roughly 2,600 square kilometres claimed in twenty-four hours against an air-superior, Gulf-financed opponent is being read either as proof that Saudi Arabia is structurally collapsing - 'expect them to lose Aden too' - or that the advance is run by Iranian officers with quiet Gulf consent. Circulating faster than either is a breaking claim that the Houthis have already taken Zuqar island and hold the entire chokepoint coastline outright, attributed to unnamed AFP and Reuters sourcing that the wires have not published in those words.
consp.spread: Multiple concurrent /pol/ threads: the coastline seizure at 142 replies, a gloating Saudi-collapse thread at 171, a 'how is this technically possible' thread asking how sandal-wearing irregulars beat air superiority, and a fresh breaking-post pushing the Zuqar claim.
consp.read: The too-fast-to-be-real instinct is doing the work, and it is the same reading applied to Kabul in 2021 and to Syrian army units in 2024. One kernel is genuinely reported rather than fringe: France 24 attributes IRGC guidance to the advance, so a hidden hand is on the wires. What the board version adds and cannot support is Gulf consent - Saudi aircraft flew strikes on Houthi positions the day before Mocha fell, which is not how a handover looks. Treat Zuqar as unconfirmed until a wire or a geolocation carries it; GeoConfirmed has placed Houthi vehicles inside Mocha, not on the islands.

brief.head: Wholesale prices jump 5.4pc as the Fed nears a hike into an oil shock
brief.h: US producer prices rose 0.4 per cent in August and 5.4 per cent on the year, with diesel up 24.1 per cent in the month accounting for over a third of the increase in final-demand goods and final-demand energy up 4.2 per cent, while core PPI printed 0.2 per cent against a 0.3 per cent forecast; futures moved from a 61 to a roughly 70 per cent chance of a Federal Reserve hike on 16 September as Brent settled near $105.26 and WTI at $100.04, both up over four per cent and Brent about 30 per cent above its early-August low, the S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth straight loss, and the ECB had already lifted its deposit rate to 2.5 per cent that morning.
brief.t: The most important number in this release is the one that did not move. Core PPI came in at 0.2 against 0.3 expected, which says August's wholesale inflation was a barrel of diesel wearing a headline number - energy did over three quarters of the broad-based rise and diesel alone did a third of the goods increase. That distinction is the whole policy question, because a central bank can raise rates against wages and it cannot raise rates against a strait. Tightening into a supply shock does not produce diesel; it produces a demand contraction that lands roughly nine months after the freight cost has already been passed through to the shelf. Two central banks are now doing it at once, and the ECB did it on staff projections whose data cut-off predates $105 oil.
brief.context: The rail is 1973 and 1979, and the honest lesson from both is that the direction of the mistake was only obvious afterwards - Burns eased into the first shock and bought a decade of inflation, Volcker tightened into the second and bought two recessions and the end of it. The desk that decides is the FOMC on 16 September, and the fact that matters about it is that three members already dissented FOR a hike in July, with PCE at 3.7 per cent and Brent at $99. The base rate for tightening into an energy supply shock is not comforting: cycles begun with crude up more than 30 per cent over two months have historically ended in recession more often than not, and Brent is up about 30 per cent from its early-August low. What would change the read is core. If September core PPI and core CPI turn up together, the Fed is deciding about wages rather than barrels, and the case for hiking stops being a category error.

angles.effect: gain - a visible response to a price level voters can see, and inflation-fighting credibility bought cheaply while the shock is external and attributable
pay - a record $5.98 national diesel average passes into food and delivered goods on a six to nine month lag, with a higher borrowing rate arriving on top of it
pays - the ten-year near 4.93 per cent and the thirty-year through 5.30 reprice the entire rollover calendar, including the 2021-22 vintage
gain - a 24.1 per cent monthly move in one product is margin for whoever owns the barrel, not cost; the diesel crack is doing the work
pay - dollar strength plus $105 crude is the classic double squeeze, and they hold a seat at neither central bank

dec.kill: Core PPI and core CPI turning up together in September. That would mean the shock has broadened out of energy into wages and services, at which point tightening is the right instrument and this read is wrong. Conversely a hike delivered on Wednesday with core still at 0.2 is a central bank raising rates against a strait.

consp.claim: That the oil move is not a war premium at all but the tape finally admitting a supply exhaustion that was already there - 'the delulu market is just slowly coming to terms that oil is running out', with $150 by year-end as the circulating target - and that the diesel record specifically is the giveaway, because distillate is the one product a strategic reserve release cannot fake. A harder strand reads the rate path itself as deliberate, an engineered squeeze on households carried out under cover of the war.
consp.spread: Diesel-record threads running simultaneously on /pol/ (60 replies) and /biz/ (90), four concurrent Stock Market Generals including one titled 'Oil barons and bobos edition', a viral Cramer clip repackaged as '$150 is about to be reality', and an 'EXIT ALL MARKETS NOW' thread.
consp.read: The peak-oil frame is doing the explaining, and the kernel worth keeping is narrower and more accurate than the claim. Distillate really is the tight link: refineries cannot switch product mix quickly, the SPR holds crude rather than diesel, and a 24.1 per cent monthly move in the one fuel that moves freight is a physical constraint rather than sentiment. What the claim cannot carry is 'running out' - OPEC+ removed its capping mechanism this year, so the binding constraint is where the spare barrels SIT, behind two contested straits, not whether they exist. The engineered-hardship strand needs no evidence and predicts nothing; discard it and keep the diesel observation.

brief.head: Supreme Court blocks Missouri's Republican map for a second time
brief.h: The Supreme Court on Thursday granted an emergency application from People Not Politicians, the group led by Richard von Glahn that gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures to force a statewide referendum on Missouri's redrawn congressional map, freezing a Tuesday order by US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, that would have required the new lines this November; the brief order carried no noted dissents and likely ends the fight, leaving the 2022 map with six Republican and two Democratic seats and sparing Representative Emanuel Cleaver's fifth district - a day after Trump told a Republican midterm convention in Dallas that every American adult would receive $5,000 if his party holds Congress.
brief.t: These are the same story told twice. Republicans hold 219 seats to 214, which makes the majority a rounding error, and there are exactly two ways to move a number that small: change who is allowed to vote for whom, or change what a vote is worth. The redistricting push was the first lever - roughly sixteen districts improved for Republicans nationally against six for Democrats - and Missouri is where it hit a wall that is not federal at all, but a state initiative process that lets voters suspend a map by petition. When the map lever jams, the money lever gets pulled, which is why a promise costing over $1 trillion arrived in the same week and why it is conditional on the RESULT rather than on need. Follow the sequencing rather than the speeches: the offer got bigger as the seat math got worse.
brief.context: The rail here is older than the fight. Missouri's initiative and referendum process dates to 1908 and was built by Progressive-era reformers precisely to give voters a veto over a captured legislature; People Not Politicians used the same instrument in 2018 and again this year, which is why a federal district judge's order ran into a state constitutional mechanism rather than a partisan objection. The deciding desk was not the full Court but Justice Kavanaugh as circuit justice for the Eighth Circuit, and the tell is that the order drew no noted dissents - an emergency posture that usually splits produced silence, which reads as reluctance to run a federal judge over a state supreme court eight weeks before an election. The base rate governs the other half: this is the third version of a direct-payment promise from this administration, after DOGE savings checks and a $2,000 tariff dividend, and neither prior version was paid. What would change the read is bill text - a sponsor, a number and a CBO score before November converts a turnout instrument into a fiscal event, and at over $1 trillion it would land on a thirty-year already through 5.30 per cent.

angles.effect: gain - a seat drawn out of existence survives, and the national redistricting arms race loses one of its clearest Republican wins with eight weeks left
gains - a state referendum instrument beat a federal district court order, a precedent other states with initiative rights will now test
pay - the map lever is spent in Missouri and the majority still stands at five seats, which is why the compensating instrument had to be larger
pay, on current evidence - the payment is conditional on an outcome and requires legislation nobody has drafted, and the two prior promises of this shape did not arrive
pays if it IS real - a trillion-plus unfunded transfer arriving during an energy shock, on a long end that just failed to respond to a tripled Treasury buyback

dec.kill: Bill text with a named sponsor and a CBO score before November kills the read that the dividend is a turnout instrument. On the map, a full-Court merits grant rather than an emergency order would mean this fight is not actually over.

consp.claim: That the size of the bribe is the confession. 'Wildly successful, popular administration, economic golden age - we don't need to buy votes, why promise 1+ trillion dollars for an assured victory?' is circulating as evidence that internal polling is far worse than the public numbers, and that the checks were floated precisely because the map lever has now failed in the courts. A second strand treats the payment itself as the attack: a $1.5 trillion transfer designed to finish the dollar, with the Covid checks cited as having already taken a third of purchasing power. A third stacks DOGE savings plus tariff checks plus the dividend into a claimed $12,000 per citizen.

brief.head: Tigray's leader says his opposition alliance is now irreversible
brief.h: Debretsion Gebremichael, TPLF chairman and the dominant figure in Tigray's politics, told Weyin Media that the opposition grouping known as Tsimdo has become institutionalised and 'irreversible', with its own leadership structure and a signed agreement among its members, and said further forces were expected to join and would be announced collectively rather than one at a time; he declined to name any member organisation. The statement lands amid renewed federal-Tigray clashes that began on 29 January and after a May gathering in Port Sudan that brought together figures including representatives of the Ogaden National Liberation Front and Andargachew Tsige.
brief.t: This is a large story that is invisible because it is not on anyone's board, and the way to read it is geographically rather than rhetorically. An armed Tigrayan structure that was never fully dismantled under the 2022 Pretoria agreement is now saying, on the record, that it has signed a written pact with insurgent and exile movements at the opposite corners of the Ethiopian state - Ogaden in the southeast, exile networks abroad. That is the difference between a regional grievance and a national one, and it is the configuration that preceded 1991. Follow the constraint rather than the character: Abiy Ahmed cannot fight in Tigray, in Amhara and in the Somali region simultaneously with a national army already rebuilt twice this decade, which is precisely why an announcement of a signed alliance with no operation attached is worth making at all.
brief.context: The rail is the Pretoria agreement of November 2022, and its load-bearing flaw was written into the text: Tigrayan forces surrendered heavy weapons and put thousands of fighters through demobilisation, but the military STRUCTURE was never dissolved, and Eritrea - whose forces fought the war - was never a party to the deal. That unfinished business is why fighting could resume on 29 January this year and why the Tigray Defense Force could withdraw from Tselemti on 1 February as a choice rather than a defeat. The desk that decides is not Addis Ababa's cabinet but whoever in Asmara and Port Sudan is willing to host and supply, because a landlocked insurgent alliance is a logistics problem before it is a political one. The base rate deserves stating plainly: announced multi-front insurgent alliances in the Horn have historically been declarations of intent that fail on command and control, and the coalition that actually took Addis Ababa in 1991 is the exception rather than the pattern. What would change the read is the thing Debretsion withheld - names. An alliance that will not publish its membership is a bargaining position; one that publishes a joint command is a war.

The industry's stated assumption is that the Houthi threat is confined to Saudi-linked tonnage; Mocha and the Hanish islands are the test of it, and a war-risk quote that stops making that distinction is the observable that converts a land advance into a world event.

Core CPI, then the FOMC on Wednesday. Core PPI printed 0.2 against 0.3 expected - the one number still saying this is an energy shock rather than a general inflation. If core turns up, the Fed is deciding about wages rather than barrels; if it doesn't and they hike anyway, they are tightening against a strait with the thirty-year already through 5.30.

Bill text for the $5,000 dividend: a sponsor, a number, a CBO score. Two prior promises of this shape - DOGE savings, the $2,000 tariff check - were announced and never paid. Absent legislation before November, this was a turnout instrument and should be scored as one.

Whether Debretsion names the Tsimdo members. An alliance that publishes a joint command is a three-front war for Addis Ababa; one that keeps its membership secret is a bargaining position. October is the window, and this is the biggest story currently off every major board.
lesson: Today's lesson is about proxies, and it explains why this board refused to raise its Iran forecast on a day when Iranian-aligned forces set Saudi oil sites on fire. When a state fights through someone else's army, it is buying a specific product: deniability. Idean Salehyan's work on the delegation of war to non-state groups sets out the trade - the sponsor gets cheapness and a plausible shrug, and pays for it with a principal-agent problem, because the proxy has its own war aims and can drag the sponsor somewhere it did not choose to go. Thomas Schelling's companion idea is that the ambiguity is not a bug: an attack nobody can cleanly attribute is a threat that is hard to answer without escalating first, which is why the wrapper is worth paying for. The base rate is where this stops being theory. On 14 September 2019, drones and cruise missiles knocked 5.7 million barrels a day - half of Saudi output - out of Abqaiq and Khurais; the Houthis claimed it, Washington publicly blamed Iran, UN monitors later found the Houthis could not have done it, and the American response was a troop deployment and sanctions, not a strike on Iran. So here is the discipline the lesson yields, and it is testable: attribution is not a trigger, ownership is. Watch whether anything hits an ASSET the United States must answer for - a US-flagged hull, an American casualty - because that, not the size of the fire in Jazan, is the variable that has historically moved American decisions.

quiz.q: Iranian-aligned forces set fire to Saudi oil facilities, and this board did NOT raise its forecast of a renewed US or Israeli strike campaign on Iran. What is the stated reason?
options: Because the attack was too small to matter to oil markets
Because in 2019 a far larger attack on Saudi oil - Abqaiq, half the kingdom's output - produced no American strike on Iran
Because the Houthis are not connected to Iran in any way
Because the US has publicly ruled out further strikes on Iran
quiz.why: The base rate is the discipline. Abqaiq removed 5.7 million barrels a day, was blamed on Iran by Washington, and produced a troop deployment and sanctions - not a strike. Damage to Saudi assets has historically not been the trigger; damage to American ones has, which is why this board's CRITICAL gate is a struck US-flagged hull or an American death rather than a burning refinery.

quiz.q: The brief says the Jazan complex is the asset that converts a Yemeni grievance into a global price. Why Jazan specifically rather than the size of any fire?
options: Because Jazan is where most Saudi crude is loaded for export
Because it is a 400,000 b/d refinery, about a tenth of Aramco's net refining capacity, and the world is short conversion capacity rather than crude
Because it is the closest facility to Iran
Because Jazan produces most of Saudi Arabia's electricity
quiz.why: A barrel of crude is not a usable product. The binding constraint in this cycle is the capacity to turn crude into diesel, so hitting a refinery bites harder per unit of damage than hitting a wellhead. Crude exports load at Ras Tanura and Yanbu, hundreds of miles from anything struck on Tuesday - which is why the brief's kill criterion is loadings, not fires.

quiz.q: Russia paused strikes on Kyiv for exactly the 72 hours that US envoys were in the region, then fired 166 drones. What does the brief say that timing reveals?
options: That Russia is running out of missiles and needed to reload
That Moscow can switch the air campaign on and off at will, which indicates confidence rather than exhaustion
That the pause was imposed on Russia by the United States
That Ukraine's air defences were down during the visit
quiz.why: A truce whose duration matches an itinerary to the hour is a scheduling accommodation, not a de-escalation - and the precision is itself the information. Fortna's finding is that ceasefires without monitors, guarantors or a demilitarised separation fail at high rates, and this arrangement had none of the three, which is why the 30-day ceasefire forecast was cut rather than raised.

quiz.q: The brief argues that stablecoins and the Fed's bill programme cannot fix Britain's 5.89 per cent thirty-year yield. What is the mechanism?
options: Because those programmes create demand for SHORT paper - bills - so the bid concentrates at the front of the curve and the long end is left to private buyers
Because the Bank of England is prohibited from buying gilts
Because stablecoins are illegal in the United Kingdom
Because thirty-year debt is not sold at auction
quiz.why: Tokenised dollar claims have to be backed by something short and liquid, which means Treasury bills. That manufactures a bid at the front end and does nothing for thirty-year duration, which is left to pension funds, insurers and price-sensitive foreigners who charge for inflation risk. Hence the brief's line that the long end is the leg no monetary innovation repairs.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. A widely circulated report puts transshipment - Chinese goods relabelled through third countries - at up to $303bn. Which observable best tests that CLAIM?
options: Whether the total Chinese trade surplus keeps rising
Whether more governments publicly endorse the report
Whether the rerouting rate holds up when customs data are matched WITHIN individual firms rather than at the product level
Whether Vietnam's exports to the US grew faster than its exports elsewhere
quiz.why: The size of the number depends almost entirely on how coarsely you match the data. Academic work found about 16.5 per cent of US-bound Vietnamese exports looked rerouted at the national product level, 6.5 per cent within provinces, and 1.7 per cent within individual firms - meaning aggregation was mistaking one company's genuine production for another's rerouting. The claim is checkable, and the check is firm-level matching.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
